newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Bangkok Bank head says Asian crisis short term.
newsitem.headline: Bangkok Bank head says Asian crisis short term.

text.p: Chatri Sophonpanich, chairman of Bangkok Bank, said the recent economic crisis in several Asian economies was only a short-term phenomenon, but it could indicate that the overall development process was not on the right track.

"A correction is needed to weed out the weak and the improper to ensure quality growth in the future," Chatri said in the text of a speech given to bankers at the International Monetary Conference (IMC).

Chatri was less worried about the ability of the Asian financial sector to weather the crisis as they have undergone a process of transformation in recent years which is not that different from other international banks.

"I am confident that banks are well able to withstand economic malfunctioning during this time of transition and therefore will remain the catalyst of economic development of countries in the emerging markets for a long time to come," he said.

However, the recent economic turbulence has given banks in emerging markets valuable lessons about open market forces and the quality of their risk assets has deteriorated immensely, pushing many to the brink of bankruptcy, he said.
Chatri said this showed that even generally-accepted capital standards are not enough to prevent mishaps and self-discipline in line with general guidelines was the only recourse left to banks.

These guidelines include: High capital-fund ratios that are above Basle Committee standards, adhere to the principle of high quality risk assets, improved cost-efficiency, maintain a square position in foreign currencies and use more domestic sources of funding.
He said the economic slowdown in many Asian countries in 1997 and problems in Korea and Thailand was mainly an adjustment process, but it could bring great pain to many in the private sector.
He said the recent attack on the Thai baht was complicated by the role of "international speculators" and came as a result of a slowdown in the Thai economy.
"When the economy is weak, devaluation speculation mounts and, at a certain point, becomes an outright attack on the currency," Chatri said.

He said the Bank of Thailand, the Thai central bank, was able to defend the first attack on the baht in February quite easily -- it has $40 billion in reserves -- but the second attack a few weeks ago amounted to a real test of the currency.
This time the impact of speculation was wider and affected both the Philippines and Indonesia, which had to resort to a costly adjustment of their own interest rates to strengthen their currencies.
